newsitem.title: USA: Healthdyne under pressure to consider bid.
newsitem.headline: Healthdyne under pressure to consider bid.

text.p: Healthdyne Technologies Corp faced new pressure Wednesday to sell the company to Invacare Corp after the hostile bidder raised its offer for the third time and hinted it might be willing to pay more in a friendly transaction.

Wall Street analysts said a large number of Healthdyne shareholders would likely be swayed by the $200 million bid, especially with no other bidder surfacing since Invacare launched its offer in January.
"The burden is on Healthdyne for some justification of why this is not a fair price," said Robert Craig, an analyst at EVEREN Securities, referring to the new $15-per-share offer.

Healthdyne has strenuously objected to a sale of the company ever since Invacare first made a $12.50-per-share cash offer in January. The bid announced earlier Wednesday raises the total price to $200 million from its previous offer of $13.50 per share, or $180 million.,
But Healthdyne's strategy, known as a "just-say-no defense," may be significantly weakened by the latest bid.
The new $15 offer "is a price point I have a heard a lot. For Healthdyne, it's going to be very tricky," said Matthew Dodds, analyst at Dillon, Read & Co Inc.

Analysts also said Invacare may be willing to pay more for Healthdyne if it agreed to a friendly deal. In announcing the latest bid, Invacare said it did not plan to raise its offer again "absent a negotiated transaction in which Healthdyne's management is able to substantiate additional value to our satisfaction."

"We had thought the previous price was a fair price, but the shareholders were being restless. This is much more than we thought we would need to pay," said a source familiar with Invacare's strategy.

Shareholders likely are growing concerned that other bidders have not materialized, analysts said. Some had thought a "white knight" would surface after Healthdyne was released last month from federal accounting rules that restrict transactions.

Dodds said Healthdyne may be worth as much as $17 per share, but the company's shareholders might be reluctant to turn down the $15 offer with no other bids on the table. Shares of Healthdyne were trading at $8.88 on the day before Invacare launched its bid.

Meanwhile, investors of Healthdyne will get their chance to talk about the takeover fight at the company's annual shareholders meeting next month. Invacare has launched a proxy fight to oust the Healthdyne board in its effort to take control of the company.
